Deepfake Video Detection Using Facial Feature Points and
Ch-Transformer

RUI YANG, RUSHI LAN, ZHENRONG DENG, and XIAONAN LUO, The Guangxi Key
Laboratory of Image and Graphic Intelligent Processing, Guilin University of Electronic Technology,
Guilin, China
XIYAN SUN, The Nanning Research Institute, Guilin University of Electronic Technology,
Nanning, China


With the development of Metaverse technology, the avatar in Metaverse has faced serious security and
privacy concerns. Analyzing facial features to distinguish between genuine and manipulated facial videos
holds significant research importance for ensuring the authenticity of characters in the virtual world and for
mitigating discrimination as well as preventing malicious use of facial data. To address this issue, the Facial
Feature Points and Class-head-Transformer (FFP-ChT) deepfake video detection model is designed based on
the clues of different FFPs distribution in real and fake videos and different displacement distances of real and
fake FFPs between frames. The face video input is first detected by the BlazeFace model, and the face detection
results are fed into the FaceMesh model to extract 468 FFPs. Then, the Lucas–Kanade (LK) optical flow method
is used to track the points of the face, the face calibration algorithm is introduced to re-calibrate the FFPs, and
the jitter displacement is calculated by tracking the FFPs between frames. Finally, the Ch is designed in the
transformer, and the FFPs and FFP displacement are jointly classified through the ChT model. In this way, the
designed ChT classifier is able to accurately and effectively identify deepfake videos. Experiments on open
datasets clearly demonstrate the effectiveness and generalization capabilities of our approach.

• Theory of computation →Structured prediction;

1  Introduction
The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology has resulted in the widespread
integration of Metaverse technology into various aspects of entertainment, daily life, and education.
Within this Metaverse environment, avatars confront substantial security and privacy challenges.
Due to the close correlation between facial features and identity information, it is crucial to
establish effective privacy protection measures through the analysis of facial features. By detecting
forged faces in the virtual world, it is possible to identify manipulated faces with malicious and
discriminatory intent, aiming to prevent gender, race, ethnic, and other imbalances. Simultaneously,
Deepfake (DF) detection can be utilized to authenticate avatars, preventing identity theft or the
deceptive misuse of avatars. If an avatar is identified as fake or manipulated, appropriate actions
can be taken to mitigate potential risks.
   Currently, DF videos, generated through adversarial networks, demonstrate an unprecedented
level of authenticity. In the Metaverse, these DF creations typically fall into three primary categories:
audio, video, and image manipulations, with video manipulations being the most widely recognized.
This technique involves recording an individual and seamlessly replacing their facial features with
those of another person using pre-existing video footage. This intricate process heavily relies on
deep learning algorithms, which effectively blend facial images and videos to produce counterfeit
content that is often imperceptible to the naked eye. It’s worth noting that current DF technology
primarily relies on Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and its optimization models for
its operation, representing a critical aspect of its functionality. ProGAN [10] and StyleGAN [16] are
the two primary methods used to generate new synthetic faces. Fake videos are mainly divided
into face replacement and expression exchange. Representative face replacement models include
DeepFaceLab [34], FaceSwap (FS) [20], Face Swapping GAN [32], and DFs [19]. These models
generate new synthetic videos by blending the image of a target person with existing video footage.
DF, also known as facial reproduction, is currently popular with techniques, such as Face2Face
(F2F) [44] and NeuralTextures (NTs) [43], where a facial expression from another person’s face
is replaced with the target’s facial expression, such as changing the expression and movement to
complete a fake “speech.” The extensive application of DF technology, as evident from this, may
pose significant security and privacy risks to virtual characters within the Metaverse.
  Given the aforementioned background, DF videos can be utilized to steal the identities of virtual
characters in the Metaverse. They can impersonate individuals for fraudulent activities, damage
others’ reputations, and initiate malicious cybersecurity attacks. This may ultimately lead to a crisis
of trust in virtual world technology. Many experts and scholars have conducted research in this
field. Currently, there are two main methods for detecting DF videos. The first method is based on
analyzing single frames of the video to determine whether it is real or fake by examining details,
such as hair, pupil, and facial features. The work presented in this article is inspired by Sun et al.
[41], who demonstrated that the jitter of facial key points between real and fake video frames
differs, as illustrated in Figure 1. Thus, a combination of Facial Feature Points (FFPs) distribution
and displacement jitter is utilized to predict whether a video is real or fake.
  We design a DF detection model FFPs and Class-head-Transformer (FFP-ChT) for the
Metaverse, which focuses on identifying inconsistencies between the distribution of FFPs on a

are as follows:

   (1) We propose a new DF detection model for the Metaverse, FFP-ChT, based on transformer for
       joint prediction of FFPs and FFP displacements.
   (2) We engineer a 468 FFPs extraction model that fuses target detection neural network and FFP
      extraction neural network, focusing on facial features and contours with high shaking rates.
   (3) We propose a ChT model specifically designed to classify video frames with FFPs. ChT trains
     FFPs and their displacements separately and jointly predicts whether a video is real or fake
      based on the two results.

2  Prior Works
As DF technology continues to evolve, the detection methods for DF videos are becoming increas-
ingly sophisticated. Currently, DF video detection can be broadly categorized into two approaches.
The first method involves analyzing individual frames of video to detect any discrepancies between

2.1  Detection of DF Videos Based on Single-Frame Images
Similar to other AI tasks, the initial detection of fake face videos using single frame images has
evolved from traditional methods to deep learning methods. Traditional methods include support
vector machines [30], co-occurrence matrices [29], residual domain differences [21], and spectral
differences [33] and have progressed to optical response heterogeneity and analysis of spatial
domain features in images [37].
   In the deep learning-based models, Jeon et al. introduced the Transferable GAN-images Detec-
tion framework, which applied transfer learning to GAN for the first time in generating image
detection [14]. Further, Jeon proposed the fine-tuning neural network architecture, Fake Detection
Fine-tuning Network, that incorporated a self-attention module to focus on the module and the
undersampling layer. This method significantly enhanced the ACC [15]. Chen et al. found that both
the luminance and chrominance components play important roles in detecting GAN-generated
facial images. Therefore, considering both the luminance and chrominance components in the
dual-color spaces can enhance the robustness of the model [5]. Hsu et al. utilized pair learning to
detect deep forged images and transformed DenseNet into a two-flow network structure, which
inputted paired information to train the common pseudo-feature network. The paired information
then connected to the classification layer to detect the authenticity of the input image. It was noted
that images generated by different GAN may have unknown image distortion, such as blur, noise,
and JPEG compression [13]. Liu et al. found that large texture information is more robust to image
distortion and proposed the GramNet model, which focuses on texture information as an essential
clue for deep forgery image detection [27]. When new DF generation methods become available,
many DF detection models’ performance deteriorates. Thus, Khalid et al. proposed One-Class
FakeDetect, which uses variational autoencoder to encode inputs as distributions in potential
spaces [18]. Hinton et al. proposed a robust architecture composed of multiple capsules to solve the
limitations of neural networks on inverse image problems. Capsule networks were applied to deep
forgery detection [36]. Dual Spatial Pyramid for Exposing Face Warp Artifacts (DSP-FWA)
model of Li et al. was limited by computational resources and production time, as the DF algorithm
could only synthesize face images of fixed size and had to be affine distorted to match the face
configuration of the source. This distortion can leave noticeable artifacts due to the inconsistent
resolution between the distorted facial area and the surrounding environment. And real face videos
and fake face videos can be classified by artifact analysis [23].
   Liu et al. proposed a new block shuffling framework that consists of intra-block and inter-block
transfer learning modules. The former improves the robustness of the network by intra-block
transformation and overfits the problem by adversarial learning, while the latter encourages the
network to learn local features through interblock shuffling and to model the semantic relevance
of local features through refactoring [26]. The model high-frequency proposed by Luo et al. in 2021
improved the detection ACC by designing a multi-scale high-frequency feature extraction module,
residual-guided spatial attention module, and cross-modal attention module [28]. Liu et al. proposed
the Spatial-Phase Shallow Learning (SPSL) model, which captures upsampled artifacts of face
forgery, improving the portability of face forgery detection [25]. Chen et al. proposed a Multi-Scale
Patch Similarity Module (MPSM) to measure the similarity between local regional features and
form a robust generalized similarity model [7]. They also proposed enhancing the “diversity” of
forgery by synthesizing enhanced forgery with a pool of forgery configurations and enhancing the
“sensitivity” to forgery by forcing models to predict forgery configurations [6]. Li et al. proposed the
face X-ray model, which can classify true and false face videos by capturing the mixed boundary of

as a classification problem based on cross-entropy loss, which emphasizes class-level differences
rather than essential differences between real and fake faces, limiting the model’s generalization
in the invisible domain [22]. Sun et al. proposed a new face forgery detection framework called
Dual Contrast Learning (DCL), which addresses the problem of local content inconsistency by
constructing local region pairs in the instance. The issue of local content inconsistency is addressed
by constructing local region pairs within the instance [39]. Gu et al. proposed the Hierarchical
Contrastive Inconsistency Learning model, which can distinguish real faces from fake faces by
deeply contrasting images [12]. In the 2022 IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern
Recognition (CVPR), Shiohara proposed a novel composite training data called Self-Blended
Images (SBIs) for detecting deep forgeries. The main idea behind SBIs is to enhance the robustness
of the detection model by generating fake samples that are challenging to identify [38]. Chen et al.
proposed a privacy-preserving model, Secure DeepFake Detection Network, which can detect DF
faces without disclosing any private inputs, thus enhancing the privacy protection of facial data
[4].

2.2  Detection of DF Videos Based on Spatio-Temporal Features of Videos
Compared to DF detection based on image detail features, there have been fewer studies on DF
detection based on video timing features, and the research in this area is relatively new. In light
of the spatio-temporal inconsistency present in generated forged videos, Zhang et al. proposed
a time-domain separation three-dimensional convolutional neural network, Temporal Dropout
3DCNN, which utilizes the inconsistent cues between video frames. This method exhibits excellent
generalization ability and ACC compared to popular benchmarks [46]. Zheng et al. proposed an
end-to-end framework comprising a full-time convolutional network. They focused on making
the network learning time-agnostic and proposed to limit the ability of the network to handle
spatial correlation. By limiting the spatial dimension, the network’s evolution concentrates on time
dependence. This method achieves better results in dataset training without any pre-training or
manual operation [48]. In 2022, Zhang et al. proposed a simple yet effective patch-level method,
spatio-temporal dropout Transformer, to fully utilize the spatio-temporal inconsistencies present
in local facial areas of different frames in DF videos. The input video is extracted into a facial
frame sequence, which is then reassembled into a patch pack and introduced into the visual
converter to learn the differential representation of dynamic spatio-temporal cues in local facial
areas describing different frames [47]. In 2021, Sun et al. proposed a Recurrent Neural Network
(RNN) classification algorithm model, LRNet, based on 68 human face landmarks, and introduced a
new plug-and-play landmark calibration module to improve the ACC of facial geometric features and
the effectiveness of time modeling [41]. Gu et al. studied the local motion of the image extensively
and proposed a new sampling unit, Intra-Snippet Inconsistency Module, which uses bidirectional
time difference operation and a learnable convolution kernel to mine short-term motion within
each fragment. Their Snippet Inconsistency Module model achieved robust results in detecting
DF videos [11]. In 2023, Sun proposed the FTDN model, which is based on facial areas such as
displacement path to detect manipulated videos. This method can robustly identify displacement
information [40].

3.1  Face Detection and FFPs Extraction
To obtain FFPs with high ACC and relatively small computational cost, the face detection model
adopts BlazeFace, a lightweight face detection model proposed by Bazarevsky et al. in 2019 [2].
The BlazeFace structure is shown in Figure 2, which mainly consists of one convolutional layer,
five Single BlazeBlocks, and six Double BlazeBlocks. The Single BlazeBlock and Double BlazeBlock
structures are shown in Figure 3.

first branch undergoes a Depthwise (DW) convolutional layer with a 5 × 5 convolution kernel,

  The BlazeFace model is used to detect the entire face in each frame of the input video and to
compute the face position in the image. The face landmark model is then employed to extract
FFPs with a detection confidence threshold of 0.5. Each FFP is defined by its position coordinates
(푥,푦), and the facial contour is outlined by these FFPs, with the landmark points aligned to their
corresponding preset positions via affine transformation, as illustrated in Figure 5. The 468 extracted
FFPs are primarily located in the eyes, nose, mouth, and face regions. The nasal region features
the highest density of FFPs in the 2D feature point distribution after the affine transformation.
The model analysis depicted in Figure 5 confirms that the selected FFPs conform to a normal
distribution.

4  Experiments
4.1  Datasets
The Faceforensics++ (FF++) dataset [35] consists of 1,000 raw videos downloaded from the
internet, along with four corresponding versions of fake faces. The dataset comprises of videos with
male and female subjects, with a ratio of 1 : 3 and 2 : 3, respectively. The resolution distribution is
as follows: approximately 1/2 of the videos are in 480p, 3/8 in 720p, and 1/8 in 1080p. All videos
contain a traceable, unobstructed front face that is used for automatic tampering to generate a real
fake face. The videos were processed using one of four automatic face tamper methods, namely
DFs, F2F, FS, NTs, and FaceShifter. As the primary aim is to assess the DF detection performance of
the designed model, the DF subset is utilized for experimentation in this study.
  Celeb-DF [24] is a recently proposed dataset with high-visual quality. The Celeb-DF dataset
comprises of two versions: Celeb-DF(v1) and Celeb-DF(v2). In this experiment, Celeb-DF(v2) version
was used. Celeb-DF(v1) contains 158 real videos and 795 fake videos, while Celeb-DF(v2) is a
significant expansion over the v1 version, with 5,639 fake videos and 590 real videos based on
publicly available YouTube clips from 59 celebrities of various genders, ages, and races. The average
length of all videos is about 13 seconds, with a standard frame rate of 30 frames per second; 56.8% of
the videos feature male subjects and 43.2% feature female subjects. The age distribution is as follows:
8.5% of the subjects are aged 60 or older, 30.5% are aged 50–60, 26.6% are in their 40s, 28.0% are in
their 30s, and 6.4% are under 30. The racial distribution is as follows: 5.1% of the subjects are Asian,
6.8% are African American, and 88.1% are Caucasian. Additionally, the dataset features a wide range
of variations in face size (in pixels), orientation, lighting conditions, and backgrounds. The fake

4.2  Experimental Environment and Evaluation Metrics
   4.2.1  Experimental Environment. The experiments presented in this article are conducted on the
Ubuntu 18.04.5 LTS operating system, utilizing a GeForce RTX 2080 Ti graphics processing unit
with a graphics memory capacity of 12 GB. The CUDA version 9.2 and PyTorch 1.7.1 framework
are utilized. The FF++ dataset is divided into a training set and a validation set using an 8:2 ratio,
similar to the basic model. For the CelebDF dataset, the division method provided by the original
authors is adopted. Additionally, the parameters used for all datasets are the same. The specific
experimental parameters are set as follows: batch size of 1.024, learning rate of 0.001, 400 epochs
for training the detection network based on the absolute location of key points, and 300 epochs for
training the detection network based on the relative location of FFPs. During training, each video
is divided into fixed 60 frame segments as a training sample. The key point information of each
frame is mapped to a 128 dimensional vector, and position coding is carried out for each 60 frame
training sample with a droprate of 0.1 for the position coding layer. Then, a Learnable embedding
vectors (cls_token) is added, and the data are passed through a Transformer encoder with a dropout
layer of droprate = 0.1 for encoding. The specific parameters for the Transformer encoder are set as
follows: the encoder had 1 layer, 8 attention heads, 512 dimensions for each attention head, 128 for
the last layer normalization, and 2 for the output of the linear transformation layer.

5  Conclusion
In this article, to improve face privacy protection in the virtual world, we presented a new method
for detecting DF videos that focuses on the inconsistency between the distribution of FFPs and
their jitter displacements in real and fake videos. Our experimental results demonstrate that the
proposed DF detection model has good robustness, as it achieves higher ACC in video datasets
with higher resolution and obtains better detection results in simple videos. With the evolution of
the Metaverse, in the future, DF detection can assist in establishing a series of identity verification
standards in the virtual world to ensure the authenticity of users’ identities. Simultaneously, it is
possible to explore DF detection that combines various sensors and data sources to enhance the
validation of real identities, thereby improving the capability to detect forged faces and reducing
deception in virtual spaces.
